title: Checkpoint: Judaism
objective: After this level you can explain how Jewish belief, scripture, law and practice fit together, from Abraham to Jewish life today.
summary: From the covenant with Abraham and the Torah at Sinai, through two Temples and their loss, to rabbis, the Talmud and the many ways Jews keep Shabbat, the festivals and kosher law today.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: from one family's journey to a worldwide people.
cards.body: Covenant, Torah, Temple, rabbis, and a life marked by days and meals. Here's the arc on one timeline, and how the pieces fit together.

events.label: Babylon destroys the First Temple; exile

cards.headline: How the pieces fit
cards.body: Jews believe the covenant began with Abraham, promised land and descendants, and took the shape of law at Sinai. That law is read aloud in a yearly cycle that never stops. When the Temple fell, Johanan ben Zakkai's academy at Yavneh set the terms for carrying on, and the Babylonian Talmud became the constitution and bylaws of Rabbinic Judaism.

cards.headline: One tradition, many voices
cards.body: Remember Level 4: every tradition is a loosely held-together family of subtraditions. Judaism shows it. In Pew's 2020 survey, 95% of Orthodox Jews kept kosher at home, and 5% of Reform Jews. A Sephardi family may keep Ladino songs, an Ashkenazi one Yiddish words, and their customs differ as a matter of tradition, not of sect.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: How Judaism grew from the covenant with Abraham and the law at Sinai into a faith of prayer and study.
Why losing the Temple in 586 BCE and 70 CE turned Jewish worship toward prayer, synagogues and rabbis.
What Shabbat, the festivals and kosher rules mean to the Jews who keep them.
Which differences are about branch, like Orthodox or Reform, and which about heritage.

questions.prompt: Put these in order: Cyrus lets the exiles return, Rome destroys the Second Temple, Babylon destroys the First Temple.

options.label: Rome, then Babylon, then Cyrus
Cyrus, then Babylon, then Rome
options.rationale: The exile (586 BCE) came before the return (538 BCE).

options.label: Babylon, then Cyrus, then Rome
Babylon, then Rome, then Cyrus
options.rationale: Cyrus (538 BCE) came before Rome (70 CE).

questions.prompt: Once completed about 600 CE, what did the Babylonian Talmud become for Rabbinic Judaism?

options.label: A record of the Temple sacrifices
options.rationale: The Temple was long gone by then.

options.label: Its constitution and bylaws
A new book added to the Torah
A history of the kings of Israel
options.rationale: It is above all a legal compilation.

questions.explanation: Completed about 600 CE, the Babylonian Talmud served as the constitution and bylaws of Rabbinic Judaism.

questions.prompt: Hanukkah's name means "dedication". What was dedicated again?

options.label: The first Torah scroll, at Sinai
Solomon's First Temple, after Babylon
options.rationale: It was the Second Temple, under the Maccabees.

options.label: The Western Wall, after Rome
The Second Temple, by the Maccabees in 164 BCE

questions.explanation: Hanukkah remembers the Maccabees' rededication of the Second Temple in 164 BCE.

questions.prompt: A family traces its customs to Spain and Portugal and sings in Ladino. What does that tell you?

options.label: Their heritage is Sephardi; it says nothing about their branch
They must belong to Reform Judaism
options.rationale: Heritage does not fix a branch.

options.label: They are Ashkenazi, from Eastern Europe
options.rationale: Ashkenazim came from the Rhineland and moved east.

options.label: They follow a different Torah from other Jews
options.rationale: The differences are in custom, not sect.

questions.explanation: Sephardim descend from the Jews of Spain and Portugal; heritage is a matter of custom, not branch.

questions.prompt: Level 4's scholars describe a faith without judging it. How does that apply to the Exodus?

options.label: Leave out the story because archaeology has not confirmed it
Describe what Jews believe, and report separately what historians find
Treat the story as proven because so many believe it
options.rationale: Belief and evidence are reported separately.

options.label: Call the story a myth, meaning it is false
options.rationale: For scholars, myth does not mean false.

questions.explanation: Bracketing sets the truth question aside: tell the story as Jews do, then say what archaeology shows.
